opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because it's happened so fast. A few years ago, if you wanted to do sentiment analysis or named entity recognition, you'd take something like a BERT-style model, fine-tune it on your task, and deploy it. It was small, it was efficient, and it did that one thing well. Now the default has become: take the biggest generative model you can access, write a prompt, and ask it to do everything.

I understand the appeal. It's convenient, you don't need labeled data, you don't need ML expertise to get started, and the results are often pretty impressive. But I think we've lost something in the shift, and we haven't really accounted for the costs.

That's actually what motivated some of our work on the energy use of inference. We compared task-specific models with these multi-purpose generative models across a bunch of tasks, like text classification, question answering, and summarization, and measured how much energy and carbon each one used. The general-purpose models were consistently far more energy-intensive, sometimes by orders of magnitude, for the same task. And they weren't always better at it. For a lot of these well-defined tasks, a small fine-tuned model was just as good or better.

So my concern is that we're using a sledgehammer to crack a nut, and we're doing it billions of times a day. Inference, unlike training, happens every time someone uses the model. When you multiply that across all the products that are now integrating LLMs into search, email, and everything else, the environmental footprint really adds up.

I'm not saying general-purpose models aren't useful. They're great for open-ended tasks, exploration, and prototyping. But I'd like the community, and especially people deploying these systems, to be more intentional: ask whether you actually need a giant generative model for this, or whether a smaller, specialized one would do the job. Right now the incentives all push toward bigger and more general, and nobody's really measuring the trade-offs. We need more transparency about energy use so people can make informed choices.

r001.rationale: The response describes a study comparing task-specific and general-purpose models across several tasks. It does not say that few tasks are studied with both approaches or that this scarcity makes empirical comparisons difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, it's a shift I've watched with a lot of mixed feelings, honestly. On one hand, I understand the appeal. When you have a general-purpose model that you can prompt or lightly adapt to do a hundred different tasks, it feels like you've collapsed a lot of engineering overhead into one artifact. You don't need a team maintaining a sentiment classifier and a separate team maintaining a summarizer. That's genuinely attractive, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

But from where I sit, working on the environmental and social impacts of these systems, I think the community has been a bit uncritical about what we're trading away. The thing about fine-tuned, task-specific models is that they were small. You could train a BERT-sized model on a single GPU, deploy it on modest hardware, and it would be really good at the one thing you needed it to do. Now we're routinely using models with hundreds of billions of parameters to do tasks like classifying whether an email is spam, and the energy cost per inference is orders of magnitude higher for, in many cases, comparable or even worse accuracy. We actually measured this. When you compare a general-purpose model doing a task via prompting against a fine-tuned model doing the same task, the general-purpose one can be dozens of times more energy-intensive, and it's not consistently better.

And I think there's a second cost that's less visible, which is epistemic. With task-specific models, you had to think about your task. You had to curate a dataset, define your labels, think about what "good" meant for your problem. That forced a kind of accountability. With general-purpose models, a lot of that thinking gets outsourced to whoever trained the base model, and we often don't know what went into it. The data isn't documented, the training choices aren't transparent, and yet we're building everything on top of it. So the research community has kind of concentrated its dependence on a very small number of models from a very small number of organizations, and I think that's a concern both scientifically and in terms of who gets to shape the field.

I'd also push back a little on the framing that this was purely a research-driven shift. A lot of it was driven by the fact that the big models were available via API and they were impressive in demos. Research followed the tooling, in some sense. That's not inherently bad, but it means we should be honest that it wasn't a careful comparison that concluded general-purpose was the right paradigm for every use case.

So where do I land? I don't think general-purpose models are going away, and I don't think they should. But I'd love to see the community reclaim a sense of proportionality. Ask what the task actually needs. If a small fine-tuned model gets you ninety-five percent of the way there at one percent of the cost, that's a legitimate and often better choice. And I'd love for us to treat efficiency and transparency as first-class research values again, not afterthoughts, because right now the incentive structure very much rewards scale over everything else.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a measured comparison of general-purpose and fine-tuned models, but does not say that few tasks are studied with both approaches or that this scarcity makes empirical evidence difficult to find.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve started treating general-purpose language models as the default, and I’m not convinced that’s always the right choice. There are tasks where a smaller, fine-tuned model can do exactly what you need, and do it with fewer resources. If you’re classifying text, for example, does that really need to be a generation problem?

The flexibility is valuable, of course. Being able to try something with a prompt lowers the barrier to entry. But I think we need to distinguish between what’s convenient for experimentation and what makes sense once you know your task. I’d like to see us ask, “What model is appropriate for this problem?” and consider efficiency alongside performance.

r001.rationale: The response favors task-specific fine-tuned models in some cases, but does not say that few researchers study both fine-tuned and multitask models or that this scarcity makes empirical comparisons difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve shifted from asking, “What model do we need for this task?” to asking, “How can we get this language model to do this task?” And those are quite different starting points. General-purpose models are interesting because you can explore a lot of capabilities without training a separate model each time. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re the best choice for every application.

If you have a well-defined task, a smaller, fine-tuned model may work just as well and require far fewer resources. So I’d like to see more emphasis on comparing those options: What accuracy do you actually need? What’s the computational cost? Does the flexibility of a general-purpose model provide something useful in this particular setting? I think there’s room for both approaches, but we shouldn’t lose sight of the problem we’re trying to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says both general-purpose and fine-tuned models have a place and calls for more comparison, but it does not mention that few tasks are studied with both approaches or that this scarcity makes empirical evidence difficult to find.
